hook: A city growing "only" 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years: twice the schools, water and roads within one generation. Growth at a steady percent speeds up as the base gets bigger. The rule of 70 lets you turn any yearly growth rate into a doubling time in your head, and the exam asks for it every year.

prereq.q: What is the percent change from 50 to 100?

figure.caption: Growing 2% a year, a population doubles about every 35 years.

chain.cause: A population grows by a fixed percent each year
chain.effect: each year’s increase is larger than the last

chain.cause: Divide 70 by the percent growth rate
chain.effect: you get the doubling time in years

chain.cause: Add the doubling time to the start year
chain.effect: you get the year the population doubles

ideas: A growth rate is the percent change per year: 2% a year means 2 more for every 100 each year.
Rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate (in %, not as a decimal).
Doubling time depends on the rate, not on the starting size.
Each doubling multiplies by 2: after n doublings, multiply by 2 n times (2, 4, 8, 16, ...).

misconception.wrong: A question asking "in what year" wants the doubling time.
misconception.right: The doubling time is a number of years. "In what year" asks you to add it to the starting year: 70 ÷ 2.5 = 28 years, so 2024 + 28 = 2052.

summary: A population growing by a fixed percent each year doubles in a fixed time. By the rule of 70, doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate in percent. Add the doubling time to the start year for "in what year"; multiply by 2 for each doubling to project the size. Doubling time depends only on the rate: twice the rate, half the time.
